articles.title: Wild report claims Apple might launch an M5 Ultra MacBook Pro
articles.subtitle: Macworld Reports about Apple switching its MacBooks and iPads to OLED displays have been circulating in the rumor mill for some time now.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Reports about Apple switching its MacBooks and iPads to OLED displays have been circulating in the rumor mill for some time now. A new report by Omdia gives us a more concrete look at when the switch could actually happen, as well as a few far-out details about Apple’s alleged plans.

The first MacBook equipped with an OLED display will reportedly be available “by the end of 2026,” according to the site, which is in line with previous rumors. The MacBook Omdia is referring to is likely to be Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro, which is expected later this year or in early 2027.

It appears, however, that the touchscreen MacBook will be a new addition to the MacBook Pro lineup, a higher-end model that could fall under Apple’s Ultra branding. Omdia states that “the existing 14.3-inch and 16.3-inch MacBook Pro models with LCD + Mini LED backlighting will not be discontinued,” which means the MacBook Pro lineup, as it is now, will continue, with Apple upgrading the chip on a regular basis.

Surprisingly, and perhaps unbelievably, Omdia predicts that this new model is “highly likely to be equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.” Apple’s M5 ultra chip is only used in the Mac Studio, which includes a complex thermal cooling system with a heavy copper heat sink that adds two pounds to the machine’s weight.

Omdia also reports that the MacBook Air will continue to use an LCD display, and that there’s a “new 13.8-inch MacBook, which is expected to launch in 2029 with a hybrid OLED display.” This “new” MacBook is likely an upgraded version of the MacBook Air, which has been reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman to be making the switch to OLED in the future.

Omida also confirms previous reports that an OLED iPad mini will arrive later this year. The current LCD iPad mini was released in October 2024, so it’s due for an update. It would be Apple’s first non-Pro tablet to have an OLED display.

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence

china

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

Introducing Wishlister, your new weekly guide to upcoming Steam games

Wishlister is a weekly newsletter bringing you a curated list of upcoming Steam games worth adding to your wishlist, sent on Tuesdays and published on the site on Fridays. You can subscribe here.

As a site that spends all day covering new games, we know all too well that there’s simply too much to keep up with. Tons of exciting games are announced every day, whether it be in social media posts that get buried by the algorithm or in showcases so loaded with content that it’s easy to forget what you just saw by the end. We wanted to help, so we made Wishlister: a weekly newsletter highlighting upcoming games that belong on your Steam wishlist.

And what a week to launch, because a very busy Gamescom just wrapped up over in Germany. The show featured tons of new games, many of which debuted on streams like Opening Night Live and Future Games Show. There were plenty of gems hidden throughout the event, so we had no shortage of games to put on your radar this week. There’s plenty more to dig through, so make sure to subscribe to Wishlister if you want a weekly refresher on what’s on the horizon.

1 Pony Island 2: Panda Circus

In 2021, developer Daniel Mullins had a breakthrough moment with the surreal Inscryption. Mainstream success hasn’t seemed to dull Mullins’ creativity, because his next game looks even weirder. Described as a “phantasmagorical voyage through time, myth, divinity, and video games,” Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is an unclassifiable game that you just need to see for yourself. All I can say for sure is that I need to play it.

2 Acornia: Mirror Worlds

Splashteam, the developers behind the excellent Pikmin homage Tinykin, is back with an eye-catching follow-up. Acornia: Mirror Worlds is part action game, part card collector, part… bakery management sim? Its delightful reveal trailer during Gamescom Opening Night Live’s preshow teased a genre-hopping adventure about an adorable little squirrel named Alva who attacks with projectiles stored in her cheeks.

Plenty of Dungeons & Dragons games ask you to kill waves of enemies, but how many are focused entirely on the downtime between battles? Dungeons & Dragons: Long Rest Tavern sees that potential, and is turning it into a cozy tavern management sim where you make life more comfortable for weary adventurers in need of a break.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: New features, release date, beta, compatible Macs
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple has already revealed many of the new features coming in macOS 27 Golden Gate, the next major update for the Mac.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple has already revealed many of the new features coming in macOS 27 Golden Gate, the next major update for the Mac. Headline changes include an all-new Siri AI assistant, major upgrades to apps including Safari, Photos, Messages, Mail and Calendar, expanded child-safety features, design refinements and performance improvements throughout the operating system. We’ve also had the chance to see many of these features in action through the beta, with the full release now likely to be only days away.

Golden Gate continues Apple’s tradition of naming macOS releases after iconic Californian landmarks. More broadly, the update represents another step in Apple’s push to make the Mac smarter and more proactive, with greater use of Apple Intelligence across the operating system and a stronger focus on helping users complete everyday tasks more quickly.

macOS 27 will support all Macs powered by Apple silicon, marking the end of the road for Intel-based Macs. While Intel models won’t be eligible for the new operating system, Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for them for some time.

Apple made developer and public betas of macOS 27 available, with the finished version expected in September 2026. This hub covers everything you need to know about macOS 27 Golden Gate, including its new features, compatibility, beta releases and Apple Intelligence upgrades.

What’s New in macOS 27 Golden Gate at a glance

Apple

Here are the top ten new features and changes coming with macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Siri AI: A redesigned conversational Siri that can answer questions, understand personal and onscreen context, access the web and take actions across apps.

Apple Intelligence: Systemwide proofreading, smarter writing tools, improved dictation and automatic file and folder naming.

Safari upgrades: Automatic tab grouping, webpage change alerts with Notify Me, AI-generated extensions and faster, more efficient browsing.

Smarter Messages and Mail: Personalized Smart Reply, better search and syncing, contextual suggestions and improved reliability.

New Photos tools: Spatial Reframing, image expansion with Extend, improved Clean Up and better search and organisation.

More powerful built-in apps: New features for Passwords, Calendar, Notes, Preview, Freeform, Weather, Shortcuts and Image Playground.

Expanded parental controls: Ask to Browse, improved Screen Time, contact approvals and broader Communication Safety protections.

Better Mac gaming: Game Porting Toolkit 4 promises significant performance and compatibility improvements for Windows games.

Refined Liquid Glass design: Better readability and consistency, adjustable transparency, cleaner Finder windows and improved iPhone Mirroring.

Faster macOS performance: Quicker app launches, Spotlight, AirDrop and networking, plus improved external-display, Thunderbolt and Bluetooth support.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: I’m an ethical muncher in The Blood of Dawnwalker, which means I’ve forced poor Coen to slurp up nine million rats
articles.subtitle: The Blood of Dawnwalker CRUNCH…ewwwwww, that’s bloody awful Coen, the half-man and half-vampire protagonist of The Blood of Dawnwalker, doesn’t like chomping down on rats.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
The Blood of Dawnwalker

CRUNCH…ewwwwww, that’s bloody awful

Coen, the half-man and half-vampire protagonist of The Blood of Dawnwalker, doesn’t like chomping down on rats.

I know this because he’s told me multiple times, after I’ve made him slurpily drain a rodent like it’s a furry Frube (other brands of tubed yoghurt are available). Sometimes he shudders a bit and makes noises of disgust. Other times he straight up says things like "This is not a nice thing to do". I know it’s not, farmboy whose family needs saving, but what’s the alternative?

I’m a long-time pescetarian in real life, and thus I’m trying to make sure his vampiric diet is at least a bit kind on the conscience. That means no going around getting his sanguine fix from friendly people. He still needs said fix though, otherwise he’ll have next to no health with which to survive fights. So, I’ve ended up having him wander off into the wilderness to find animals he can drain during breaks in the action, while also taking cheeky nibbles out of foes mid-scrap.

I appreciate that, from a food ethics perspective, this is basically akin to letting someone commit murder provided they don’t use a nuke to do it. Still, I feel I’ve got to draw the line somewhere in order to remain more hero than villain in a fashion that’ll mean Coen can still look at himself in the mirror. Well, look at himself in the mirror during daytime, at night I’d assume he might not show up on account of the whole vampire business.

The game itself doesn’t judge me regardless of how I get Coen the gulps of red juice he needs, and perhaps a bit counterintuitively, that’s made it a stronger RPG.

Rather than having a Red Dead Redemption -style honour notification cartoonishly pop up whenever Coen does something morally questionable, or having a meter stashed in the menus grind closer to the end which says ‘evil bastard’, each transgression is met with silence beyond the likes of Coen’s occasional outbursts about rats and the panicked squeal of a deer or goat as he plunges his fangs into it.

I’m left to wonder if the modus operandi I’ve devised in order to be the least evil vamp possible are actually any better than mindlessly feeding on whatever, whenever.

Does this poor lad from Laslea, once wholly human and devoted to helping his family get through the days, still have that valiant soul despite the dark sickness that’s been thrust upon him? In a lot of games, I feel like I wouldn’t so much be asking this question as much as the game would be telling me the answer.

There’s undeniable RPG choice and consequence in doing something you know’s a bit dodgy or downright evil and watching a number of gauges on the great machine surrounding your character start to tick closer towards ‘utter bellend, this one’. However, it can be just as effective sometimes if the only stewing over your actions is left to take place in your own head.

Am I a bad person for forcing poor Coen to crack open plague-ridden critters like they’re cans of beer? Am I any better a person for making sure he’s well-satiated before he heads into town, lest he drain someone mid-chat? Should I be letting him feed on the poor fools he’s fighting against, who’re often human soldiers that call the valley home just as Coen does? Is it right to walk up the sides of buildings and warp onto their rooftops when that’s likely putting a perfectly good staircase out of work?

Meanwhile, embracing Coen’s vampiric powers is most certainly a boon in terms of making a more effective tool to fight the other vrakhir oppressing his home and holding his family hostage. His vampire form’s far more powerful than his human one, especially early on.

Teamed with the 30-day ultimatum Dawnwalker puts on Coen’s quest, that power’s seriously seductive in a way it wouldn’t be if human Coen wasn’t a bit useless or his vampire form came with more built-in downsides. Unless you get careless, there aren’t many practical drawbacks to exploiting being a bloodsucking blight on the Earth.

So, rather than being slapped about the face with condemnations, you’re left with only the gentle, but regular, prodding of the narrative to remind you that you’re often leading Coen deeper and deeper into similar habits the creatures he’s fighting against have.

You can do as I’ve generally done and try to find some moral boundaries you won’t cross, throwing away vrahkir blood that can grant new abilities and simply killing Brencis’ Boyars rather than sapping their power. You can stick to the wilderness as much as possible while in your beastly form, obscuring your hideous nature from civilisation by retreating behind a wall of tree cover or rocky gorges.

You’ll still be reminded of what you’re doing to Coen, what you’re making him do, and just how horribly unnatural some of it is.

Every rat drained with a grimace is one step closer to salvation for those Coen loves. But all that’s staring him in the face immediately after doing it is a limp corpse flopping to the ground, where it’ll be left to attract more flies than it already has buzzing around it. Most RPGs serve their final triumph atop a mountain of dead bodies, but Dawnwalker’s done a more haunting job of making me confront that on a minute to minute basis than a lot of its peers.

articles.title: M6 vs. M5 Pro Mac Mini Buyer's Guide
articles.subtitle: Apple last week announced two new Mac mini models, one with the all-new M6 chip and one with the M5 Pro chip that debuted in the MacBook Pro earlier this year.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple last week announced two new Mac mini models, one with the all-new M6 chip and one with the M5 Pro chip that debuted in the MacBook Pro earlier this year.

Somewhat like the ‌MacBook Pro‌ last year, Apple has again placed its newest silicon in the entry-level machine and a previous-generation Pro chip in the high-end machine, so the more expensive ‌Mac mini‌ is not simply a faster version of the cheaper one. The M6 model starts at $899 with a 12-core CPU, 16GB of unified memory, and 256GB of storage. The M5 Pro model starts at $1,699 with a 15-core CPU, 24GB of memory, and 512GB of storage, and it can be configured with up to an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU.

Both are the highest starting prices Apple has ever set for the ‌Mac mini‌, which makes the $800 gap between the two models more consequential than in previous generations. Our guide helps to answer the question of how to decide which of these two ‌Mac mini‌ models is best for you.

Both models are available to pre-order now and launch on Tuesday, September 22. The two machines are physically identical and share the majority of their hardware. The shared features include:

The same 5.0 by 5.0 inch aluminum enclosure in silver, unchanged since 2024

Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, a first for the ‌Mac mini‌

Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via the N1 chip, another first for the ‌Mac mini‌

2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, with a 10Gb Ethernet configuration option

Two front USB-C ports and a headphone jack with high-impedance headphone support

An HDMI port and native support for up to three external displays

Genlock over USB-C for synchronizing a display with a camera such as the iPhone 17 Pro

macOS 27 with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI

Everything that differs between the two models is set out below:

For the majority of buyers, the M6 model is the right choice, and not only because it is $800 cheaper. It is the newer chip, built on a 2nm process, and Apple says it contains the world's fastest CPU core. It is also the only ‌Mac mini‌ with the Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which Apple says delivers up to twice the peak compute of the single Neural Engine used in the M5 Pro.

If your workload is dominated by everyday productivity, web work, photo editing, coding, or light on-device AI, the M6 should feel marginally faster in day-to-day use, especially for single-core tasks, and be more future-proof.

Buying the more expensive machine means accepting older silicon in exchange for a broader performance. What the M5 Pro provides is scale rather than speed per core: up to 18 CPU cores against 12, up to 20 GPU cores against 12, and 307GB/s of memory bandwidth against 170GB/s. Those advantages only really surface in sustained, heavily parallel work such as video rendering, 3D and VFX production, compilation of large codebases, and scientific simulation.

The memory ceiling is the clearest dividing line. The M6 model tops out at 32GB of unified memory, while the M5 Pro reaches 64GB. If you intend to run local large language models, work with complex 3D scenes, or keep sizeable datasets resident in memory, the M6 configuration simply cannot be specified high enough, no matter how much you spend on it. Storage works the same way, with the M6 limited to 2TB and the M5 Pro extending to 8TB.

Thunderbolt is the other hard limit. The M5 Pro model has three Thunderbolt 5 ports, double the bandwidth of the Thunderbolt 4 ports on the M6 model, and Thunderbolt 5 is what allows several ‌Mac mini‌ systems to be clustered together to run large AI models entirely on device. This is significant for users building a small local compute setup, or attaching high-speed external storage arrays for video work.

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker's mods immediately scrap the time pressure mechanic, which is apparently a dealbreaker for some people
articles.subtitle: That didn't take much time.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
The Blood of Dawnwalker 's out now—which means that players are getting introduced to its slightly more experimental take on RPG time. For the uninitiated, protagonist Coen has about 30 days and nights to save his family, the ticking clock of which is tracked in the UI. Completing quests, levelling up, and ticking off side-objectives costs "time segments".

The idea, then, is to make it so that players have to (quite literally) spend their time wisely. In practice, this system doesn't have much in the way of actual teeth, acting more as a means to dissuade you from going all completionist on the map. In my playthrough, I've currently killed two out of three of Brencis' lieutenants and I still have 20 comfortable days and nights to spare.

Which is probably why some folks have decided to opt out entirely. The " Better Story Timer " on Nexus Mods has options to triple the already-generous 30 day limit to 90 days, makes it so that perks and skills don't cost any time to obtain, and increases the number of segments in a day from eight to a whopping 32.

This essentially means Coen can take his sweet time, pun intended, moseying around the Vale Sangora without a care in the world while his family rot in a dungeon somewhere. The mod already has over 13,000 downloads, hinting that a lot of folks don't appreciate the ticking clock in their open world RPG.

On the one hand, I sort of get it. The Blood of Dawnwalker's time pressure is, given the game's current generosity, a bit of a fib that mostly just gets in the way of you exploring the map at your own pace. It does have some interesting implications, mind—and I do enjoy being steered towards day-only activities and night-only questlines to keep things interesting.

On the other hand, if you strip those same time mechanics from The Blood of Dawnwalker entirely, it just becomes… well, a pretty decent open-world RPG, but pretty unremarkable. Regardless of my critiques of the system, the time mechanic is one of the most noteworthy things the game has going for it.

Still, it's a controversial feature, and it's no wonder that the posts section of the mod already has around 300 comments in there, most of which can be summed up by "thank god".

Personally, I think Rebel Wolves would do well to include some optional modifiers in the menu—though not because I'm one of those people, actually, quite the opposite. I sort of wish I had less time to complete my tasks. I think having modifiers for relaxed or more tense playthroughs would be a great addition to the game.

Metaphor: ReFantazio got me hooked on the interesting tension that comes from having to manage time pressures, and I think The Blood of Dawnwalker would be a slightly more interesting game if it was meaner. As does Shaun Prescott in our The Blood of Dawnwalker review, who wrote: "In the end, Dawnwalker doesn't have the courage to allow this system to show its fangs. I feel like if it did, we’d have a modern classic on our hands."

articles.title: Petit Planet's delightfully cosy galactic take on Animal Crossing is the closest we'll ever get to the life sim on PC
articles.subtitle: Everyone's favourite cosy sim, now with gacha.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
I had a lot of one-hour appointments at Gamescom, but none of them had time escaping from me quite like my 60 minutes with Petit Planet. It's Hoyoverse's attempt to tap into the Animal Crossing demographic, and by that I mean the developer has essentially taken Nintendo's cosy life sim and shot it up into space.

I was honestly flabbergasted at how brazen the whole thing was. From the text boxes, to the character animations, to the little audio jingles that accompany them—near enough everything (bar its cosmic setting) screams Animal Crossing. But you know what? I kinda loved it.

Like I mentioned, Petit Planet transports the cosy vibes traditionally reserved for land and sea and instead puts them in galactic pastures. That doesn't mean I'm locked out of biomes found on terra firma, though. After making my human character and being greeted by a delightfully pink bunny, I'm given two planets to pick from—one that's more your traditional forest-y vibes, and one that's significantly more desert-like.

I picked the former, of course—though it looks like you might have even more starter options in the future—and set to work on building up a little planet of my own. I got to do all the traditional social sim stuff: catch fish and bugs, shake trees to dislodge their fruit (plums, in my case), and make friends with the furry cast who launched themselves onto the planet alongside me.

As I progress more tasks, Petit Planet's landscape unfurls before me. I don't arrive with a beach to fish at, but I get one shortly after catching enough bugs to pop into a little magical eco-tank. I suppose it serves a similar purpose to the museum, in that you can drop all your first-time catches in there, though there aren't big shiny exhibits to walk around.

Doing all of this fills a jar that I can use to water a tree and progress my planet further to get new areas like the beach, or get the capacity to invite new neighbours. My time with the demo saw farmer fox Yunguo take an interest in my new galactic home, where we planted crops together before being given the ability to pop her house right next to my own.

Unfortunately I didn't get to play around too much with decorating in Petit Planet, but unlike Animal Crossing I have full 360 degrees of reign over where I can place and rotate my own house and the houses of my space villagers. There'll undoubtedly be tons of cute decor pieces I can smatter across my planet, too, which I'm incredibly excited about.

The one thing I didn't manage to get a feel for is just how gacha'd out the wazoo Petit Planet is going to be. The game's pre-registration gifts at least signal some kind of currency palooza, and I assume it'll go down some sort of character banner route for potential villager candidates.

I know it's Hoyoverse's bread and butter, but I do hope the gacha side of things doesn't encroach on the relaxing life sim part too much. The two things feel like oil and water, you know?

I am willing to play a lot more of Petit Planet to find out, which shows just how badly the game got its hooks in me in such a short amount of time. It's potentially the closest thing we'll ever get to Animal Crossing on PC, after all—and that status alone makes it worth my time. And probably my money.

articles.title: Apple to Mac developers: It’s time to let go of Intel
articles.subtitle: Macworld When Apple introduced its M-series chips, it also marked the beginning of the end for software written for Intel Macs. It’s been nearly six years since then, and Apple has let developers know that they can bring Intel Mac development to a close.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
When Apple introduced its M-series chips, it also marked the beginning of the end for software written for Intel Macs. It’s been nearly six years since then, and Apple has let developers know that they can bring Intel Mac development to a close.

In an email to developers, Apple said:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers. By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

When Apple announced macOS 26 Tahoe last year, the company said it would be the last version to support Intel Macs. This new announcement takes another step toward dropping Intel altogether. A new Apple support document adds this vital bit of information:

macOS 27: Final release to support Rosetta — Intel-only apps will no longer run on Mac computers with Apple silicon after this update.

Now it’s up to developers to determine when to stop with Intel code. App designers will need to determine how many of their users still use Intel Macs before they can drop development, which means that some will need to continue to support Intel for a while. If you use an Intel app, reach out to the app developer to find out their plans.

articles.title: Perplexity Introduces ‘Hybrid Compute’ for Computer Agent on Apple Silicon Macs
articles.subtitle: Source: Perplexity. Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based. Recently, Perplexity also introduced Portable Computer, a local-first version of Computer that can escalate work to the cloud with a user’s permission.

Hybrid compute approaches the problem from a different direction. Tasks start in the cloud but if a new local classifier detects potentially sensitive information, the user is alerted and asked whether they want to route it to a local model, although users also have the option to let the flagged data be used by a frontier cloud-based model. Gemma E4B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, and a Perplexity post-trained version of Qwen3.6 35B are available at launch for that local work, with more models to come in the future.

Tasks that don’t require sensitive information are handled in the cloud by frontier models that also orchestrate the cloud and local tasks. Users select the cloud orchestrator and Perplexity chooses the helper frontier models used.

Another key feature is that hybrid compute works with tasks begun from an iPhone or iPad, too. Those devices could already kick off a session, but now they can also run tasks that use sensitive information locally if your Mac is turned on and running Perplexity.

Yesterday, I got a demo of the feature that walked through three scenarios:

an attorney researching a legal brief, with sensitive client data on their Mac, allowing them to update it locally,

an analyst using web-based data to update a confidential slide deck for a presentation about a company’s financials, and

a small business owner kicking off pricing research from her iPhone that was combined with private pricing data for her business that never left her Mac.

I haven’t tried hybrid compute myself yet, but if it works as advertised, it’s a big step forward for Perplexity, and one that a lot of its competitors are also chasing. AI agents are only as good as the tools and data to which they have access.

Tool calling has been a big focus over the last year and more, but data privacy is an equally important issue that needs to be solved before more companies, especially those in regulated industries, adopt agentic tools like Personal Computer. It’s good to see Perplexity tackling this head-on.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Xbox Is Putting a Time Limit on Cloud Gaming
articles.subtitle: All great things come to an end Xbox is watering down Game Pass benefits to cut costs. Starting in November, cloud gaming will receive a major overhaul, and one of the most notable changes is the time limit that will be assigned to each Xbox account depending...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
All great things come to an end

Xbox is watering down Game Pass benefits to cut costs. Starting in November, cloud gaming will receive a major overhaul, and one of the most notable changes is the time limit that will be assigned to each Xbox account depending on its Game Pass subscription tier. Cloud gaming has been one of the subscription's selling points, so it is a shame to see it being downgraded.

In 2023, Xbox projections suggested that cloud gaming would be Game Pass's main selling point. However, these projections also showed that there would be nearly 80 million Game Pass subscribers by 2026, and this was not the case. Considering that cloud gaming is nowhere near as popular as Xbox wanted it to be, it will be the target of Xbox's next cost-cutting operation.

Game Pass Ultimate subscribers only get 15 hours of 'free' cloud playtime a month

Starting in November, Xbox is implementing monthly time limits on cloud gaming across all Game Pass tiers. Game Pass Ultimate subscribers will get up to 15 hours of cloud gaming, Premium subscribers will receive 10 hours, and Essential subscribers will get a mere five hours. According to Xbox, these changes supposedly stem from the costs of rising cloud playtime and a larger cloud gaming player base. But oddly enough, Xbox reassures players that this change will only affect 4% of subscribers.

On the bright side, players will be able to access Xbox's cloud gaming services without subscribing to Game Pass. Playtime will be available for purchase on the Xbox Store. It appears that bought hours will be cumulative, but it is unknown if those granted to subscribers on a monthly basis will carry over time and remain available when their subscription runs out.

Cloud playtime restrictions have just been announced, and more details will be revealed in the future. Then, we will be able to evaluate how impactful this will be and whether paid cloud hours will be too expensive for regular users to continue using the service. In November, Xbox will share information about cloud gaming's cost per hour, additional eligible games, and price differences across regions.

Polygon's Aris Notis predicted in July that Game Pass's price decrease would most likely mean that its best features would be diluted due to CEO Asha Sharma's Xbox reset. As Notis wrote: "The likely downstream effect of Xbox’s restructure on Game Pass is starting to shape up like everything else has in 2026: You get less for more".

This happened with day-one releases, which were previously available across all tiers but eventually became exclusive to Game Pass's highest tier. Now, it's happening with cloud gaming.

For the same price, fans will have access to fewer hours on the cloud, and if they wish to get more, they will have to pay up. Xbox promises that cloud gaming is being put behind a paywall so it can continue to improve its reliability and performance. So, hopefully, players can expect a better experience when they start paying for their extra playtime in the cloud.

articles.title: Apple’s loaded September kicks off with ‘huge launch’ next week
articles.subtitle: Macworld September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more. This year is especially monumental.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more.

This year is especially monumental. It’s the first month and the first event helmed by new CEO John Ternus, the release of the biggest OS updates in years with an all-new Siri, and the unveiling of Apple’s first folding iPhone. All that and more are coming this September. Here’s what’s on the way.

New CEO, new iPhone, and more

As of September 1, Tim Cook is out as CEO (taking a backseat role as Chairman) and new CEO John Ternus is at the helm. That means the big Apple event on September 9 will be the first not headlined by Cook in 15 years. In his welcome letter to employees, he promised a “huge launch that’s going to be phenomenal.

” With Ternus at the helm, will the Surprise and Shine event be different in tone or structure from what we’ve seen the last few years? We’ll find out on September 9 at 10 am. Here’s what we expect at the event:

iPhone Ultra: The marquee product of the new lineup will be Apple’s first foldable device, likely to be called iPhone Ultra. We already have a good idea of its design, but we don’t yet know about its features, particularly what Apple is doing with the software. We expect the price to top $2,000.

iPhone 18 Pro/Max: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be an evolutionary upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro. The big updates are a faster A20 Pro processor and a new main camera with variable aperture.

Apple Watch Series 12: We don’t expect much to be new about the Apple Watch Series 12. There should be a faster processor, and Apple is said to be bringing back the ceramic case option, but the rumors say not to expect a change to the design or major new features this year.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: Just like the Series 12, the new Ultra is going to be primarily a “chip and ship” update with no major design changes or new features.

Apple’s iPhone event will be loaded with shiny new products—and hopefully some surprises.

Apple

AirPods 5: Apparently, there’s an AirPods 5 that could ship as early as September. Like AirPods 4, it would come in both standard and active noise-cancelling versions, but we’re not sure what will actually be new. This is not expected to be the AirPods with cameras in them, and it’s unknown what the new features might be.

Apple TV 4K: A new-generation Apple TV box with a new processor that supports the new Siri AI is supposed to ship before the end of the year. It could be announced at the September event, or it could just go up on the website one day. There’s plenty of time for this update to be released in later months, too.

HomePod mini: Just like the new Apple TV box, the main reason for this to exist is to get a new chip that supports Siri AI. As with the Apple TV, this may not even get mentioned at the event at all and could just go up on the website as an update anytime this year.

Smart home hub: The biggest question mark for Apple’s upcoming event is whether or not the company will unveil its new home hub device. This is said to be a tablet-like pad, with a new 7-inch squarish shape, that will come in both base/speaker-mounted or wall-mounted varieties. It will run a new operating system that blends some of the features of Apple Watch and Apple TV.

It’s meant to control your smart home stuff, make FaceTime calls, listen to music, and so on. Rumors say it could launch this fall, but that doesn’t necessarily mean September.

Mac mini and Mac Studio: While announced in August, the new M6 / M5 Pro Mac mini and M5 Max/Ultra Mac Studio are actually shipping starting on September 22.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
The Blood of Dawnwalker

Also, some blacksmith now knows how to craft a holy sword

Witcher-flavoured vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker has received its first post-launch patch, with developers Rebel Wolves dipping their fangs into a modest neckful of problems with blocked quest progression and general controller behaviour on PC. They've also taught a blacksmith a new recipe.

Alas, the devs are still working on fixes for those problems with stuttering, PlayStation button-mapping, and shader compilation we covered last night. Still, at least your brother Lunka will no longer get hopelessly lost while walking you through the tutorial.

Out now on PC, the patch also has a fix for Farkas (pictured above), the resentful jester you'll need to talk to for a certain major quest. Hitherto, Farkas might refuse to speak to you if you murdered all the NPCs around him. Rebel Wolves have wheeled him backstage and ordered him to stop being so picky. Which is to say, you can kill everybody now without making it impossible to proceed with the quest.

The most enigmatic of the patch highlights concerns the Uriashi blacksmith, who appears in a more elusive quest I won't spoil. He's "learned how to craft a certain holy sword", it seems. I'm not sure if that's a bugfix or a new feature, but I'm happy for the guy. Finally, there are some PC-specific "adjustments to controller dead zone and input issues while sprinting". Can't think of anything funny to write about those. Maybe "undead zone, amirite?"

A few technical whoopsy-doodles notwithstanding, Blood of Dawnwalker appears to be a very good RPG, though people are already modding its main quest timer to save themselves a bit of deadline stress. I've also read a lot of carping about the cutscenes being capped at 30fps. You young people don't know you're born. Back when I were a lad, we'd be lucky to get 30 frames a year.

Each frame had to be hand-excavated from freezing mountain soil and delivered to your home by a team of mules. It took my family six generations to get past the opening arrow wall in Tomb Raider.

Apple announced the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini on August 25, 2026, with sales beginning September 22. For most buyers, we recommend the M6 Mac mini. Starting at $899/£899, it is considerably more expensive than the M4 generation, which launched at $599, but it offers improved performance for everyday work, office tasks, coding, photo and video editing, and general creative use. Should you buy a Mac mini now?

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

articles.title: Nvidia puts its money where its mouth is on open weight AI, moving to buy Hugging Face for $13 billion
articles.subtitle: Come on guys, fling a few mil my way?
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Nvidia has just announced that it intends to acquire Hugging Face, the biggest open platform dedicated to developing machine-learning applications. Considering Nvidia has been all-in on AI for the past few years—to the point that I barely remember the last time the company even mentioned gaming in an earnings call—it's hardly a surprising move.

What did encourage a sharp intake of breath from me though was the price of this purchase; Nvidia will buy Hugging Face for a total of $12,930,300,000. $11.9 billion of that will go to Hugging Face's investors, while employees that join Nvidia will be offered an ‌equity-based retention ⁠program of up to $1 billion, according to Reuters. But even though there's billions of dollars in the mix, that doesn't mean the walls are about to come down around Hugging Face.

"Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang writes, "Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want. Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face."

He adds that the platform will continue to support both open source and open weight AI models. This is something Huang demonstrably feels passionate about, as he dedicated his first ever X post to defending easy access to open AI models.

In today's announcement, Huang further elaborates, "Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch. They enable organizations to match the right model to the right job. That is how AI can advance safely, strengthen cybersecurity and sovereignty, accelerate innovation, and reach factories, hospitals, farms, classrooms and Main Street businesses around the world.

"AI advances faster when people can build together."

Hugging Face was most recently in the news when a number of OpenAI's models breached an isolated test environment and hacked the development platform's internal network. OpenAI has since detailed how it's protecting itself from the kinds of attacks its own models carried out.

Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue told CNBC last week that the company approached Jensen Huang about a deal a few weeks ago. He described Nvidia as a "perfect home". "During the summer, I think we realized that Hugging Face and open source AI in general was at the turning point, and that it needed more, more resources, more scale, more visibility."

For those keen on an agentic, local AI future, this deal could well be good news; it is arguably the biggest consumer-facing resource for free downloads of local AI models as well as retrained and abliterated models.

With Nvidia set to soon release its first RTX Spark laptops with entirely its own silicon inside—from CPU to GPU cores—its own focus is obviously on putting local AI in the hands of consumers as well as frontier AI in the hands of multi-billion dollar orgs. Keeping a platform such as Hugging Face rolling makes complete sense.

The nearly $13 billion deal is Nvidia's second largest to date. First place goes to the $20 billion Non-Exclusive Inference Technology Licensing Agreement with chipmaker Groq, though it looks like Nvidia's AI inference GPU still won't see the light of day this year. Nvidia's RTX Spark 'superchip', with purported RTX 5070-like performance, may arrive sooner rather than later.

Our Andy rubbed his greasy mitts all over a host of RTX Spark laptops at Gamescom, though there's still little word on pricing. Here's hoping the RTX Spark laptops only make my eyes water in the best possible way when they go on sale in October 2026. But realistically, they ain't going to be cheap.

articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Miami-Dade police outraged by proposals to turn parts of Miami into GTA 6, saying that Rockstar's game embodies what they "work every single day to prevent"
articles.subtitle: The mayor of Miami-Dade, Florida has been pitching Rockstar Games about transforming parts of the county into recreations of areas from Grand Theft Auto 6, in the face of complaints from law enforcement and members of the judiciary.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
The mayor of Miami-Dade, Florida has been pitching Rockstar Games about transforming parts of the county into recreations of areas from Grand Theft Auto 6, in the face of complaints from law enforcement and members of the judiciary. GTA 6 is itself inspired by Miami, so yes, this is one of those "simulation colonising reality" situations.

The proposed publicity event would include "an immersive arrival experience" at Miami International Airport. with signs for Vice City and planes coated in GTA 6 livery, together with branded Metromover skytrains and specially designed manhole covers.

It's a predictable bid to snaffle a few of those GTA marketing dollars, while driving up the regional circulation of affluent Vice City nuts. Also predictable: a few people, and specifically the cops, find the idea of their neighbourhood being mocked up to resemble a Grand Theft Auto game problematic.

Miami-Dade sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz and commissioner Juan Carlos Bermudez have already spoken out against the potential deal, observing in a joint statement that "we should be promoting the Miami-Dade we have worked so hard to build, not a fictional version of our community defined by crime and violence. ”

According to SpaceXAI’s announcement, Grok Bot is a new kind of AI agent described as “AI teammates you can give real work to.”

Each Bot gets its own computer, then signs into the apps and services you already use to take on work across inboxes and other tools.

SpaceXAI says Bots can complete jobs end to end, only returning when approval is needed.

You can message one “like a colleague,” the company says, and the agent will remember conversations, learn preferences, and improve with more use.

Grok Bot launches in beta today on Mac and iOS. Windows and Linux desktop versions are also available. Android is listed as coming soon.

Access is initially restricted to SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra, and Cursor Teams Premium subscribers.

You can learn more from the official announcement here.

Yahoo Finance was one of those to attribute the slide to the WWDC announcements.

articles.title: 8 Near-Perfect Anime To Watch if You Like 'Solo Leveling'
articles.subtitle: These underdog stories make for exciting power fantasies Some anime stories rely on exaggerated power fantasies to prop up a stand-out protagonist, but Solo Leveling takes it to another level.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
These underdog stories make for exciting power fantasies

Some anime stories rely on exaggerated power fantasies to prop up a stand-out protagonist, but Solo Leveling takes it to another level. This trope can take many forms when used for sustained dramatic effect in genres like shonen or isekai. Shows like One-Punch Man come alive thanks to satirical deadpan humor while still delivering on the power fantasy.

Others, like The Eminence in Shadow, embrace a ludicrous brand of self-aware absurdity. By contrast, Solo Leveling, which is based on a fantasy web novel by Chugong (later adapted into an immensely popular manhwa), uses addictive dungeon-crawler elements and RPG-style power progression to keep things dynamic and interesting.

In Solo Leveling, gifted Hunters fight vicious beasts to protect humanity, but the notoriously weak Sung Jin-woo finds himself trapped in a hopeless survival loop. Whereas the power levels of all Hunters are fixed, Jin-woo is chosen by the enigmatic "System" and is given the ability to accrue experience points and level up. In theory, there are no limits to what he can achieve.

While no anime shares an exact premise with Solo Leveling — namely, the gamification of power in an urban fantasy dungeon-crawler — these below entries also indulge in high-octane action in a dynamic world inspired by fantasy or video game mechanics. Without further ado, here are the nine best anime worth checking out if you like Solo Leveling.

9 Tomb Raider King

Based on the Korean web novel and manhwa by Sanji Jiksong, Tomb Raider King might be the closest spiritual successor to Solo Leveling on this list. Mysterious tombs have appeared around the world, each containing powerful relics drawn from mythology and history. Ruthless corporations quickly turn their recovery into a lucrative industry, employing raiders like Seo Joo-Heon to brave the tombs on their behalf.

After his employer betrays him and leaves his team to die, Joo-Heon awakens 15 years in the past — shortly before the first tombs emerge — with his memories and expertise intact. He uses that advantage to claim the most valuable relics for himself and exact revenge on the people who exploited him.

Tomb Raider King trades Sung Jin-woo’s steady level progression for a time-travel power fantasy built around foreknowledge, elaborate traps, and supernatural artifacts. But its Korean source material, modern dungeon-raiding economy, and increasingly overpowered protagonist make the similarities impossible to miss.

8 Shangri-La Frontier

In Shangri-La Frontier, Rakuro Hizutome loves playing “trash games” — glitchy, mass-produced VR titles that are notoriously clunky. After experiencing burnout, Rakuro takes a stab at playing Shangri-La Frontier, the acclaimed full-dive VR game that is all the rage.

After being transported into the game world, Rakuro assumes the bird-masked avatar Sunraku and is confident that his skills will help him master this challenging reality. Unfortunately, the path ahead in such a polished world is rife with truly dangerous obstacles, which often lead to in-game nerfs that can manifest after a player character is cursed.

While Shangri-La Frontier leverages stat-based progression and strategic min-maxing like Solo Leveling, it is much more lighthearted in its exploration of gamer culture and dramatic stakes.

7 Log Horizon

Based on the light novel series by Mamare Touno ( Maoyu ), Log Horizon also centers on an MMORPG named Elder Tale with a massive player base. Unlike Sword Art Online, which uses real-world VR mechanics to fuel its premise, Log Horizo n transports unwitting players to the game world after they log in to play the latest expansion pack.

Enter our socially awkward protagonist, Shiroe, who bands together with his friends Naotsugu and Akatsuki to combat the challenges ahead. While most players are already aware of how the game world functions, what was once a thrilling pastime suddenly becomes a game of life and death.

This might sound like more of the same, but Log Horizon ’s emphasis on teamwork and tactical prowess is a breath of fresh air for those who enjoy exploring nuanced socio-political tiers in video games.
